Spatial Visualizations

What are geo-data?

…and in which contexts play geo-data a role in the field of social sciences?

data characterised by a geographic location or referring to a geographic location 🌍

Types of geodata

[1] absolute geo-data

  • GPS data 📍
  • projection via a coordinate reference system (CRS) 🗺️

What are geo-data?

Types of geodata

[1] absolute geo-data

  • GPS data 📍
  • projection via a coordinate reference system (CRS) 🗺️

[2] relative geo-data

  • “at home” 🏠
  • dominating the human use of geo-data 💬
  • \(\rightarrow\) need to be connected to other types of geo-data

Structured and unstructured geo-data

  • structured: organization of the data facilitates processing by computer (e.g. shapefile format of vector data) 👨‍💻️

  • unstructured: geo-information must first be extracted using methods such as geocoding, geotagging or geoparsing 🕵️

Import of spatial data: sf objects

  • Overview
  • Example
  • Output
  • “Simple Features” objects are data.frames
  • additional dimension to each observation: certain type of geoinformation (geometry column), e.g. 
    • points (described by one pair of coordinates) 🔵
    • Lines (described by two coordinate pairs) ➖
    • Polygons (described by at least three coordinate pairs)
    • “Regular Grid” (described by a pair of coordinates for the center of gravity + grid size)
# Create a sub-directory
directory_name <- "./data"
ifelse(dir.exists(directory_name),
        "Directory exists", 
        dir.create(directory_name)
        )

# download shapefile of electoral districts during Federal Election 2021 (zip file)
temporary_file <- tempfile()
bundeswahlleiter_link <- "https://www.bundeswahlleiter.de/dam/jcr/8794eadd-fc0c-4889-a233-2ccae3b4cf5e/btw21_geometrie_wahlkreise_geo_shp.zip"
download.file(bundeswahlleiter_link, temporary_file)
unzip(zipfile = temporary_file, exdir = paste0(directory_name))
unlink(temporary_file)
electoral_districts_shp <- read_sf("./data/Geometrie_Wahlkreise_20DBT_geo.shp")
head(electoral_districts_shp)


# which crs?
sf::st_crs(electoral_districts_shp)

Visualisation of spatial data

  • Overview
  • Example
  • Output
  • “normal” dataframe
  • additional column: geometry
  • spatial data can be easily visualized with ggplot
  • the corresponding ggplot layer is called geom_sf
  • ✔️ using geographical information, we can link a variety of different (unrelated) data sources
ggplot(data = electoral_districts_shp) +
    geom_sf() +
    theme_bw()

Linking spatial data to other data sources

  • Overview
  • Example
  • Output
  • any data that shares an identifier with the sf data can be linked
  • identifiers can carry implicit spatial dimension, e.g.:
    • country name
    • state names
    • electoral districts
  • BUT: just because data can be mapped does not always mean it should be mapped?
  • How to avoid being fooled by maps
electoral_data_url <- "https://www.bundeswahlleiter.de/dam/jcr/2a90d988-7063-48af-b265-dfb9fa14f7e3/btw21_kerg2.csv"
electoral_data <- read_csv2(electoral_data_url,
                            skip = 9) %>%
  filter(Gebietsart == "Wahlkreis") %>%
  filter(Stimme == 2) %>%
  filter(Gruppenname == "AfD") %>%
  rename(electoral_district_id = Gebietsnummer,
         party = Gruppenname,
         afd_vote_share = Prozent) %>%
  select(electoral_district_id,
         party,
         afd_vote_share)

head(electoral_data)

# generate character id to match the data to the shape file
electoral_districts_shp <- electoral_districts_shp %>%
  mutate(electoral_district_id = str_pad(
    as.character(WKR_NR),
    pad = "0",
    width = 3,
    side = "left"
  ))

# left_join (!) to shape file
electoral_districts_shp <- electoral_districts_shp %>%
    left_join(.,
        electoral_data,
       by = c("electoral_district_id")
       )


# plot the vote share of AfD
afd_vote_plot <- ggplot(data = electoral_districts_shp) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = afd_vote_share)) +
  theme_void() + 
  scale_fill_distiller(transform = "reverse",
                       name = "AfD Vote Share")
afd_vote_plot

Contrasting different spatial distributions

  • Overview
  • Example
  • Output
  • use patchwork to show two spatial distributions side-by-side
# add the official socio-demographic information for the electoral districts
structural_data_url <- "https://www.bundeswahlleiter.de/dam/jcr/b1d3fc4f-17eb-455f-a01c-a0bf32135c5d/btw21_strukturdaten.csv" # nolint
structural_data <- read_csv2(structural_data_url,
                           skip = 8) %>%
  rename(electoral_district_id = `Wahlkreis-Nr.`,
         electoral_district_name = `Wahlkreis-Name`,
         foreigner_share = `Bevölkerung am 31.12.2019 - Ausländer/-innen (%)`) %>% 
  select(electoral_district_id,
         electoral_district_name,
         foreigner_share) %>%
  # keep only observations that relate to electoral districts
  filter(!str_detect(electoral_district_name,
                     pattern = "[Ii]nsgesamt"))


# add the share of foreigners to the shape file 
electoral_districts_shp <- electoral_districts_shp %>%
  left_join(.,
            structural_data,
            by = c("electoral_district_id")
  )

# plot the share of foreigners
foreigner_share_plot <- ggplot(data = electoral_districts_shp) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = foreigner_share)) +
  theme_void() + 
  scale_fill_distiller(direction = 1, 
                       palette = "BuGn",
                       name = "Share of Foreigners"
                       )
foreigner_share_plot


# show both plots side-by-side
afd_vote_plot + foreigner_share_plot +
    plot_layout(guides = 'collect')

Text and Annotations

Why Annotate?

  • Overview
  • Example
  • Output
  • data visualization is not just about plotting data, but about communication
  • a plain plot shows what is in the data, but it doesn’t offer any interpretation (forces the reader to do all the work).
  • an annotated plot guides your reader, by highlighting key findings, providing context, and turning a simple ‘chart’ into a compelling ‘insight’.
  • we use annotations to:
    • Highlight important points or groups (e.g., outliers).
    • Explain anomalies or trends.
    • Label key features directly.
# Just the raw data. What are we supposed to see?
plot_before <- ggplot(
    bikes,
    aes(x = temp, y = count)
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5, color = "grey60") +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    title = "Before: Just the Data",
    subtitle = "Reported bike shares vs. air temperature",
    x = "Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Reported bike shares"
  )

# Same data, but now with a story.
plot_after <- ggplot(
    bikes,
    aes(x = temp, y = count)
  ) +
  # 1. De-emphasize the unimportant points
  geom_point(alpha = .5, color = "grey60") +
  # 2. Highlight the important points
  geom_point(
    data = filter(bikes, count > 40000),
    color = "firebrick",
    size = 2
  ) +
  # 3. Add a rectangle to group the outliers
  annotate(
    geom = "rect",
    xmin = 17,
    xmax = 22,
    ymin = 42000,
    ymax = 54000,
    color = "firebrick",
    fill = NA,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  # 4. Add text to explain the highlight
  annotate(
    geom = "text",
    x = 19.5,
    y = 41000, # Positioned just below the box
    label = "What happened on these days?",
    color = "firebrick",
    size = 4,
    vjust = 1
  ) +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    title = "After: A Clear Insight",
    subtitle = "Annotations guide the reader to the most important data points.",
    x = "Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Reported bike shares"
  )

# Use patchwork to show side-by-side
plot_before + plot_after

The Text & Annotation Toolkit

  • ggrepel ➡️ For clean, non-overlapping labels. It intelligently “repels” text from data points and other labels.

  • ggtext ➡️ For rich text styling. It lets you use Markdown and HTML to add bold, italics, and colors to your titles, subtitles, and labels.

  • ggforce ➡️ For highlighting and enclosing groups of points with geom_mark_hull, geom_mark_rect, etc.

  • geomtextpath ➡️ For placing text labels directly onto a line, following its curve.
